grammar_notes.title: Talking About the Past ('dzakaunganidzwa')
grammar_notes.content: The verb 'dzakaunganidzwa' expresses a completed past action. Shona has two main ways to talk about the past: 1) For actions that happened earlier today or very recently, combine the short subject prefix ('nda-' = I, 'wa-' = you, 'a-' = he/she, 'ta-' = we, 'va-' = they) directly with the verb stem (e.g., 'ndamuka' = 'I woke up today', 'wabudirira' = 'you have succeeded'). 2) For events that happened yesterday or further in the past, insert '-ka-' after the subject prefix (e.g., 'takatenga' = 'we bought', 'vakaenda' = 'they went', 'akadanidzira' = 'he shouted').
grammar_notes.rule: Recent Today Past: [nda- / wa- / ta- / va-] + verb | Earlier Past: [ndaka- / waka- / taka- / vaka-] + verb

grammar_notes.title: Actions Happening Right Now: The '-ri ku-' Progressive
grammar_notes.content: To describe an action that is happening right now ('I am doing', 'it is raining', 'they are walking'), Shona uses the helper verb '-ri' ('am/is/are') followed by 'ku-' ('to') and the action verb. For people, the forms are 'ndiri ku-' (I am), 'uri ku-' (you are), 'ari ku-' (he/she is), 'tiri ku-' (we are), and 'vari ku-' (they are). In fast speech or writing, the two words are sometimes joined together (e.g., 'ndiri kuenda' or 'ndirikuenda').
grammar_notes.rule: [Subject + -ri] + ku-[verb] -> Ndiri kuverenga (I am reading) | Vari kufamba (They are walking) | Mvura iri kunaya (It is raining)

grammar_notes.title: Colours & Describing Objects in Shona ('dzitema')
grammar_notes.content: This passage uses colour vocabulary such as 'dzitema'. Shona has three traditional core colour adjectives that change their prefix slightly to match the noun they describe: '-chena' (white/clean, e.g., 'ruvara ruchena' or 'shangu chena'), '-tema / nhema' (black/dark, e.g., 'mota nhema' or 'ruvara rutema'), and '-tsvuku' (red/bright brown, e.g., 'mota tsvuku' or 'ruvara rutsvuku'). For other colours like green ('girinhi'), blue ('bhuruu'), or orange ('orenji'), speakers typically say 'ruvara rwe-' ('the colour of...') followed by the colour name, as in 'ruvara rwegirinhi' (green).
grammar_notes.rule: Core Colours: -chena (white), -tema / nhema (black), -tsvuku (red) | Phrase pattern: ruvara rwe-[colour] (e.g., ruvara rwegirinhi)

cultural_notes.title: Dress, Grooming & Personal Presentation in Zimbabwe
cultural_notes.content: Neat personal presentation ('kuchena') is highly valued in everyday Zimbabwean life—whether dressing for work, church, school, or visiting family. Notice how 'hembe' refers broadly to a shirt or top, 'mbatya' (or 'nhumbi') means clothes in general, and 'shangu' means shoes. Braided hairstyles ('bvudzi rakarukwa'), earrings ('mhete'), and sun hats ('ngowani') are also everyday topics of compliment and description.

active_exercises.prompt: Translate this new sentence into English: 'Mukoma wangu akatenga mota chena nezuro.'
options: My sister is wearing a red dress today.
Which bus goes to the city centre?
My older brother bought a white car yesterday.
The black truck is parked beside the road.
active_exercises.correct_answer: My older brother bought a white car yesterday.
active_exercises.explanation: 'Mukoma wangu' = 'My older brother', 'akatenga' = 'bought', 'mota chena' = 'a white car', 'nezuro' = 'yesterday'.

active_exercises.prompt: Why is 'white' written as 'chena' in 'hembe chena' (white shirt), but 'machena' in 'mabhuku machena' (white books)?
options: 'Machena' means light grey while 'chena' means bright white
Only clothing can use the word 'chena'
'Machena' is only used in the past tense
Colour adjectives change their prefix to match the noun they describe ('ma-' for 'mabhuku')
active_exercises.correct_answer: Colour adjectives change their prefix to match the noun they describe ('ma-' for 'mabhuku')
active_exercises.explanation: In Shona, traditional colour stems (-chena, -tema, -tsvuku) take the prefix of the noun they describe.

active_exercises.correct_answer: Good morning Father, how did you wake up?
active_exercises.explanation: 'Mangwanani' = 'Good morning', 'baba' = 'Father', and 'mamuka sei?' = 'how did you wake up?'.
